headline: Men Walk On Moon
summary: Apollo 11's lunar module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquillity at 20:17:40 UTC on 20 July 1969. Neil Armstrong stepped onto the surface about six and a half hours later, and Edwin Aldrin followed some twenty minutes after him, while Michael Collins stayed in orbit aboard Columbia.
body:
Armstrong partly flew the final descent by hand to clear a crater, and Eagle came to rest about four miles beyond the predicted point on a level, rock-strewn plain. The two men worked outside for more than two and a half hours: they photographed the site, collected lunar material, deployed experiments, planted a flag stiffened by a horizontal rod and read a plaque fixed to the ladder strut. They were on the surface for twenty-one hours and thirty-six minutes before the ascent stage lifted to rejoin Columbia.

The mission answered a commitment made in 1961 and was funded inside a Cold War competition. Newspapers made different meanings from the same day: contemporary reporting led with the landing and the scale of television attention, while later retrospectives set the achievement beside Ralph Abernathy's protest at Cape Kennedy over poverty and racial inequality. The landing time, the crew roles and the surface work are recorded facts; the claim that the flight resolved anything on Earth is interpretation.
context: The Moon has no atmosphere. The sky above the site stays black in full sunlight, shadows fall hard and unsoftened, there is no wind to move fabric, and disturbed dust travels in clean ballistic arcs before settling. The Sun sat low in the east over the landing area, and the ground is a relatively smooth plain of fragmental debris.
contentNote: The world stages the extravehicular activity of 21 July, which is what the anchor photograph documents. The touchdown itself is a separate, earlier moment and is described rather than staged.

world.subject: A white Apollo pressure suit with a gold-visored helmet, its gloved hands held in the near foreground on the grey regolith plain of the Sea of Tranquillity.

anchors.object: United States flag on a horizontal rod

world.environment: Fine grey regolith cut with deep boot treads, small craters and angular blocks, a black sky, hard shadows, harsh low sunlight.
world.style: Hasselblad colour film, high contrast, grain, 1969.
world.idle: The suited figure stands still on the regolith, weight settled, the gloved hands steady in the foreground as sunlight glares off the white fabric and a thin film of grey dust clings along the boots.
world.travel: Boots press crisp treads into the grey dust in slow low-gravity strides, flicking small arcs of grains that fall straight back onto the surface as the regolith slides past underfoot.
guards: the sky above the horizon stays black in full sunlight, the way an airless sky reads on film

events.name: Kick the regolith
events.detail: The boot in the foreground scuffs forward through the grey dust and throws a fan of grains ahead of it; the grains travel in clean straight arcs and land in a sharp-edged spray, then the boot settles back onto the surface.

events.name: Read the ladder plaque
events.detail: The gloved hands reach toward the plaque fixed to the ladder strut of the lunar module, the engraved lettering and the two hemispheres of the Earth catching the low sunlight across the brushed metal, and the hands lower again.

events.name: Set out the solar wind collector
events.detail: The gloved hands lift the folded foil sheet of the solar wind collector into frame, unroll it and set its frame upright on the regolith, the foil rippling once and holding still in the hard sunlight while the boots stay planted.

vertical.jump: The suited figure pushes off the regolith and rises in a slow low-gravity hop, boots lifting clear of the dust and hanging a moment before settling back down onto the surface.
vertical.crouch: The camera lowers toward the ground as the suited figure crouches down low over the regolith, the gloved hands coming close to the boot-printed dust.
vertical.stand: The suited figure straightens back up out of the crouch.
